name: Mahakashyapa
role: Foremost in ascetic practice; led the First Council
summary: In Buddhist tradition, Mahakashyapa was a wealthy brahmin who gave everything up to follow the Buddha. He became the leader of the monks after the Buddha's death and presided over the First Council.
about: Buddhist texts say Mahakashyapa was born Pippali into a rich brahmin family in Magadha and married Bhadda Kapilani, with whom he agreed to live as a celibate. Moved by the suffering of small creatures in their fields, they both gave up their wealth. He met the Buddha under a fig tree and exchanged robes with him, an honour no other disciple received. The Buddha called him foremost in ascetic practice. After the Buddha's death, tradition says he called and led the First Council to gather the teachings. Later legends, in several traditions, say he rests in a mountain cave to await the future Buddha Maitreya. Chan and Zen also name him as the first patriarch of their line.
kidSummary: Mahakashyapa was a very rich man who gave up all his money to follow the Buddha. He lived simply and was famous for staying strong and cheerful with very little. After the Buddha died, he helped gather the teachings so they would not be lost.

story.title: A rich young man
story.text: Pippali was born into a wealthy family. He did not want to marry, so he shaped a golden statue of a perfect woman and said he would wed only someone just like it. His parents sent brahmins to search, and it led them to Bhadda Kapilani. Both wanted a life of learning, not riches, so they agreed to live as friends.

story.title: Tiny creatures
story.text: One day Pippali saw birds eating worms in his fields, and Bhadda saw the same with insects in hers. They felt sad that their farms were causing this, and decided to give away all they owned.

story.title: Under the fig tree
story.text: Pippali met the Buddha sitting under a fig tree and became his student. The Buddha swapped his robe for Pippali's fine one, a rare honour.

story.title: Living simply
story.text: Mahakashyapa chose to live with the fewest things, even when he was old. The Buddha said he was foremost in simple living.

story.title: Keeping the teachings
story.text: After the Buddha passed away, Mahakashyapa gathered monks in a cave near Rajagaha. The monks learned the teachings by heart and recited them together, so that they could be handed down by memory to everyone.

teaches: Keeping wise words safe for others
places: Fig tree between Rajagaha and Nalanda

facts.text: The Buddha's funeral pyre would not catch fire at first. Pali accounts say gods held it back until Mahakashyapa arrived to pay his respects, and then it lit by itself.
He heard of the Buddha's death from a wandering ascetic carrying a flower of the heavenly coral tree, which was said to be lying all over the place where the Buddha had died.

To put off marrying, young Pippali made a golden statue of a perfect woman himself and told his parents he would only wed someone just like it. He hoped no such woman existed, but the search found Bhadda Kapilani.
The two agreed to live as friends rather than spouses, laying a garland between them at night.

At the crossroads he took the right-hand road and she the left. Tradition says the earth shook as they parted, and the Buddha, sensing a great disciple was on his way, walked about five miles to meet him.
The Buddha swapped robes with him, a gesture with no earlier example, which tradition reads as marking him as the monks' future leader.
The Buddha's robe was a patched rag-robe, said to have been taken from a charnel ground; its value came from being worn by the Buddha.
When the Buddha's feet were honoured at the pyre, texts say they came out of the many layers of cloth wrapping the body so that Mahakashyapa could bow to them.

He sought out the very poor so they could earn merit by giving. In one account a leprous woman's finger fell into the food she offered, and he ate it anyway. In another he found a woman near the end of her life.

He presided over the First Council, held in a cave near Rajagaha in the first rainy season after the Buddha's death, and reportedly kept Ananda out of it until Ananda reached enlightenment the night before.
In the Chan and Zen story of the Flower Sermon, the Buddha held up a flower and only Mahakashyapa smiled. Modern scholars think the tale was composed later to give Chan its own lineage.
Later texts say he sits in a cave beneath Mount Kukkutapada wrapped in the Buddha's robe, waiting for the next Buddha, Maitreya.
The legend says the mountain closed around him, and when King Ajatashatru and Ananda visited, it opened just enough to show his body.
In one account, he hands the robe to Maitreya and then bursts into flames.
Inspired by this legend, a Japanese religious leader named Jikigyo starved himself in a small cell, hoping to meet Maitreya as a mummy.
A later Theravada text says he collected the Buddha's relics from families, hid them in an underground chamber, and Ashoka later divided them into 84,000 portions.
Some Tibetan sources say he learned of the Buddha's death from an earthquake, and that he first warned a court brahmin so that King Ajatashatru would not die of shock at the news.
Texts praise him for supernatural powers on top of his strict forest life. Sources differ on his meditative absorption: some rank him equal to the Buddha, others only just below.

When the Buddha suggested that, now he was old, he could ease his strict habits and stay near him, Mahakashyapa politely declined. He said the practices helped him and would set an example for later monks.

He urged his former wife to leave a group of wandering ascetics and become a Buddhist nun, and got the Buddha's leave to share half his alms food with her. Some monks complained, but she became an arahant and praised him in a poem.

Once 500 goddesses offered him food and he refused so poor people could have the merit. Sakka, king of the gods, then posed as an old weaver and offered rice. Mahakashyapa saw through it and told him off for taking the poor's chance.

quiz.q: What did the Buddha give Mahakashyapa that was unusual?
quiz.why: The Buddha swapped robes with him, which no other disciple was said to receive.
He is called foremost in ascetic practice.

quiz.q: Which meeting did he lead after the Buddha died?
quiz.why: He presided over the First Council in a cave near Rajagaha.

quiz.q: Who does the legend say Mahakashyapa is waiting for in a mountain cave?
quiz.why: Maitreya is the future Buddha in Buddhist tradition.
